3: Subsequent-events procedures (auditing). After the balance sheet date the auditor looks for events that affect the statements being audited. Typical procedures: read the latest available interim financial statements and compare them with the statements being audited; inquire of management about unusual adjustments and new commitments; read minutes of meetings; obtain a legal letter; obtain a management representation letter. Tests of internal controls, cutoff tests and inspection of inventory belong to the audit of the period itself.
6: Bond premium amortisation. Over the whole life of a bond issued at a premium, the total premium amortised equals the premium, whichever method is used. The straight-line and effective interest methods differ only in how much is amortised in each year. At maturity the carrying amount of the bond equals its face value under either method, and the total interest expense recognised over the life is the same.
19: Client acceptance (auditing). Before accepting an engagement the auditor evaluates the integrity of management. Management placing limits on the auditor's access to information the auditor needs is treated as an indicator that management may lack integrity. Unusual business results or accounting events are matters for risk assessment and audit planning, and do not by themselves cast doubt on management's integrity.
24: UCC Article 2 (sales). A firm offer is a signed writing by a merchant that gives assurance it will be held open. It is irrevocable for the time stated, or for a reasonable time if none is stated, but never longer than three months, even without consideration. Unless the offer says otherwise, an acceptance is effective when it is sent by a reasonable means of communication (the mailbox rule), and a revocation is effective only when received.
81: Tax return preparer penalty (IRC section 6694). For a position that is not a tax shelter and is disclosed, a reasonable basis is enough. For an undisclosed position, substantial authority is needed. For a tax shelter or a reportable transaction, the preparer must reasonably believe that the position would more likely than not be sustained on its merits. The penalty applies when the standard for the situation is not met.
109: Governmental reporting. The statistical section of a comprehensive annual financial report presents trend information. It covers many years, commonly ten fiscal years, and shows financial trends, revenue capacity, debt capacity, demographic information and operating information. The financial statements report the current fiscal year, with prior-year comparison.
166: Property received by gift (IRC section 1015). The donee generally takes the donor's basis. If the property's fair market value at the date of the gift is less than the donor's basis, the donee uses the donor's basis to compute a gain on a later sale, and uses the fair market value at the date of the gift to compute a loss. If the sale price falls between the two figures, no gain or loss is recognised.
174: Compilation engagements (nonissuers). A compilation provides no assurance. An accountant may compile statements that omit substantially all disclosures if the report says so and the omission is not intended to mislead users. A lack of segregation of duties and a lack of internal control do not prevent a compilation. An accountant should not accept an engagement when management's integrity is in doubt, for example when indications of misappropriation are not investigated by management.
194: Basis of a partnership interest (IRC sections 722 and 752). A partner's basis in a partnership interest received for contributed property equals the partner's adjusted basis in that property, reduced by the amount of the partner's liabilities that the partnership assumes, net of the partner's share of those liabilities (a decrease in a partner's share of liabilities is treated as a cash distribution). A partner's basis cannot be below zero.
267: Compilation reports (nonissuers). In a compilation the accountant presents information that is management's representation, and gives no assurance. If the statements omit substantially all disclosures, the report must say so. A standard compilation report that does not mention omitted disclosures implies that the statements include all the disclosures that the applicable financial reporting framework requires.
